inputs.need:
I am the lead nurse for the heart failure service at a 380-bed district general hospital. We follow about 540 patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and most of them are not on the target doses of the four medicine groups the guideline recommends: a beta blocker, an ARNI or ACE inhibitor, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor. When we checked the clinic list in June, only 61 of 214 patients seen in the previous six months were on at least half the target dose of every medicine they could take. Doses are changed at cardiology appointments every four to six months, so titration takes a year or more, and several patients were readmitted while still on starting doses.

Our two heart failure specialist nurses are independent prescribers and have asked to run a nurse-led titration clinic: fortnightly visits or telephone calls, blood tests before each change, and a written protocol agreed with the consultants for when to increase, hold or refer. The cardiologists support it but want to know whether it is worth setting up as a service or whether we first need to study it ourselves.

What I need help with is deciding this honestly: what the published evidence already shows about nurse-led titration, whether anything about our setting means we cannot rely on it, what we should measure once the clinic runs (doses reached, safety events such as high potassium, low blood pressure and kidney function changes, readmissions, patient experience), and how to present this to the directorate without overclaiming. We have no research funding and do not want to create extra work for patients or staff that does not help them.
inputs.constraints: No research funding. The two nurse prescribers can give up to 6 clinic hours per week between them. Any new clinic must fit the existing heart failure service staffing and the trust's non-medical prescribing policy.

records.title: Nurse-led titration of heart failure medicines versus usual cardiology follow-up: a randomised comparison in two hospital clinics
records.authors: Achterberg-Moyo L, Castellane-Idris P, Rhee-Okafor D
records.abstract: Background: many patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction remain on starting doses of guideline medicines. Methods: in two hospital clinics we randomly allocated 262 patients to titration by heart failure nurses with fortnightly visits and a written protocol, or to usual cardiology follow-up every three to four months. Results: at 6 months, 58 percent of patients in nurse-led titration and 31 percent in usual follow-up were on at least half the target dose of both a beta blocker and a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor. Hospitalisation for heart failure within 12 months occurred in 9 percent and 16 percent (hazard ratio 0.54, 95 percent CI 0.30 to 0.97). Potassium above 6.0 mmol/L occurred in 3 percent of patients in each group. Conclusions: nurse-led titration reached higher doses sooner without more hyperkalaemia.

records.title: Nurse-led titration clinics for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.authors: Vasquez-Holm R, Oduya-Pritchard K, Lindqvist-Amadi S, Tanaka-Browne E
records.abstract: We searched four bibliographic databases to March 2021 for studies comparing titration led by nurses with physician-led titration in adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. In total, 11 studies with 2,480 patients met the criteria, seven of them randomised. Nurse-led titration increased the proportion of patients reaching target doses (risk ratio 1.62, 95 percent CI 1.31 to 2.00) and reduced all-cause hospitalisation (risk ratio 0.78, 95 percent CI 0.66 to 0.93). The effect on mortality was imprecise (risk ratio 0.88, 95 percent CI 0.70 to 1.10). Protocols differed in visit frequency and in the medicines titrated, and no included study titrated SGLT2 inhibitors. Risk of bias was moderate in most randomised studies because outcome assessment was not blinded.

records.title: Titrating four medicine classes in a nurse-led heart failure clinic after SGLT2 inhibitors became available: a service evaluation
records.abstract: We describe the first 176 patients treated in a nurse-led titration clinic that titrates a beta blocker, a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor or ARNI, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor. Visits were fortnightly, alternating clinic and telephone, with blood tests before each dose change. The median time to the best tolerated regimen was 14 weeks. At 6 months, 71 percent of patients were taking all four classes and 52 percent were on at least half the target dose of each. Potassium above 5.5 mmol/L led to a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist being held in 11 percent of patients, and eGFR fell by more than 30 percent in 4 percent. There was no comparison group, and patients who declined referral were not followed.

records.title: Patients' experience of telephone and clinic visits for heart failure medicine titration: an interview study
records.abstract: We interviewed 22 patients who had completed medicine titration in a nurse-led heart failure clinic. Patients valued seeing or speaking to the same nurse and understanding why each dose changed. Frequent blood tests were the main burden, especially for those who relied on others for transport. Several patients aged over 80 preferred clinic visits to telephone calls because they found it hard to describe dizziness over the phone. Patients who had been admitted during titration often linked the admission to a dose change, whether or not the change was the cause. The findings suggest offering a choice of visit type and explaining in advance how many blood tests titration will need.

records.title: Safety of rapid up-titration of heart failure medicines in the 90 days after discharge from a district general hospital
records.authors: Farouk-Dunmore S, Ahlberg-Chukwu O, Pereira-Nash J
records.abstract: We reviewed 140 consecutive patients discharged after a heart failure admission who started nurse-supported up-titration within two weeks. Over 90 days, symptomatic hypotension that led to a dose reduction occurred in 7 percent, potassium above 6.0 mmol/L in 2 percent and a fall in eGFR of more than 30 percent in 5 percent. No death was judged related to titration by two reviewing cardiologists. Readmission for any cause within 90 days occurred in 18 percent. Patients aged 80 or over had more dose reductions for hypotension. The study had no comparison group and relied on hospital results, so tests done in primary care may have been missed.

records.title: Competences for non-medical prescribers who titrate heart failure medicines: a consensus framework
records.authors: Heart Failure Nurse Prescribing Working Group
records.abstract: A working group of heart failure nurses, pharmacists and cardiologists agreed by a two-round consensus process the competences a non-medical prescriber needs before titrating heart failure medicines without a doctor's review of each change. The framework lists 18 competences in four domains: assessment of congestion and blood pressure, interpretation of potassium and kidney function results, dose adjustment rules for each medicine class, and referral thresholds. It recommends a written titration protocol signed off by a named cardiologist, supervised practice for the first 20 patients, and a review of safety events every six months. The framework does not report outcomes and predates the routine use of SGLT2 inhibitors.

records.title: Deprivation, travel distance and missed titration visits in a heart failure nurse service
records.abstract: We examined 612 patients referred to a heart failure nurse titration service over three years. Missed titration visits were more common in the most deprived fifth of neighbourhoods (24 percent of scheduled visits) than in the least deprived fifth (9 percent). Patients living more than 20 miles from the clinic missed more visits and took longer to reach their best tolerated regimen. After the service added telephone visits with blood tests at community sites, the gap in missed visits between the most and least deprived fifths narrowed from 15 to 6 percentage points. Patients who needed an interpreter were under-represented among referrals compared with the local heart failure population.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A randomised comparison and a systematic review of 11 studies agree that nurse-led titration raises the proportion of patients reaching target doses and lowers hospitalisation; the pooled studies predate SGLT2 inhibitors. Two service reports from district settings describe four-class and post-discharge titration with potassium-related holds and dose reductions but few serious events, without comparison groups. Patients value continuity and dislike frequent blood tests, and missed visits are commoner in deprived areas, a gap that telephone visits narrowed. The effectiveness question is answered well enough to act on; local safety with four classes and equitable access are what remain to monitor.
response.gradeRationale: Randomised and pooled evidence with a consistent direction for doses reached and hospitalisation, downgraded for unblinded outcome assessment and for indirectness to four-class titration with SGLT2 inhibitors. Safety and access findings come from uncontrolled service data and are low certainty on their own.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims recorded with passages; overall certainty moderate.

response.reading: Doses stall because every change waits for a consultant slot, while the retrieved evidence shows that nurse-led titration with fortnightly contact moves doses faster and reduces admissions. The fourth medicine class raises the monitoring load: potassium and kidney function must be checked before changes, which is where the community blood test sites matter. Access is unequal: missed visits cluster in deprived neighbourhoods and among patients far from the hospital, and patients over 80 may need face-to-face visits. Governance rests on the signed-off protocol and the prescribing policy.

response.designSummary: Descriptive monitoring of a new service against a pre-opening baseline; no hypothesis test.
response.sampleSize: All referred patients are included; about 120 patients are expected in the first year at 6 nurse hours per week. At 120 patients, a proportion of 60 percent has a 95 percent confidence interval half-width of about 9 percentage points, enough to see whether the clinic is far from the baseline of about 29 percent. No sample size calculation is needed because no comparison is tested.

response.secondaryAnalysis: Counts and rates of hyperkalaemia, symptomatic hypotension and eGFR falls per 100 patients titrated; missed visits by deprivation fifth; heart failure admissions within 12 months, described.

response.title: A nurse-led titration clinic for heart failure medicines in a district general hospital: service evaluation plan
response.abstract: Aim: to raise the proportion of patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction on at least half the target dose of every indicated class from about 29 percent to 60 percent within 6 months of referral. Setting: a district general hospital heart failure service. Intervention: fortnightly nurse-led titration under a signed-off protocol. Measures: doses reached, hyperkalaemia, hypotension and kidney function falls, missed visits by deprivation. Results will be reported after 12 months of operation.
response.introduction: Randomised and pooled evidence shows that nurse-led titration raises doses and reduces admissions. The local question is whether a new clinic reaches these results safely and equitably, not whether nurse-led titration works.
response.methods: Registered service evaluation. All referred patients are counted; measures are defined before opening and reported monthly with 95 percent intervals against a six-month baseline from the clinic list.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present monthly cohorts, balancing measures and missed visits by deprivation fifth.
response.discussion: The discussion will compare local results with the retrieved randomised and service reports and state what the service changes next.
response.limitations: No comparison group; referral selection; primary care results may be missed.
response.conclusion: To be written after 12 months; it will describe the service and will not claim a causal effect.
response.summary: Service evaluation report structure with results left empty.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am the lead nurse for the heart failure service at a 380-bed district general hospital. We follow about 540 patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and most of them are not on the target doses of the four medicine groups the guideline recommends: a beta blocker, an ARNI or ACE inhibitor, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor. When we checked the clinic list in June, only 61 of 214 patients seen in the previous six months were on at least half the target dose of every medicine they could take. Doses are changed at cardiology appointments every four to six months, so titration takes a year or more, and several patients were readmitted while still on starting doses.

Our two heart failure specialist nurses are independent prescribers and have asked to run a nurse-led titration clinic: fortnightly visits or telephone calls, blood tests before each change, and a written protocol agreed with the consultants for when to increase, hold or refer. The cardiologists support it but want to know whether it is worth setting up as a service or whether we first need to study it ourselves.

What I need help with is deciding this honestly: what the published evidence already shows about nurse-led titration, whether anything about our setting means we cannot rely on it, what we should measure once the clinic runs (doses reached, safety events such as high potassium, low blood pressure and kidney function changes, readmissions, patient experience), and how to present this to the directorate without overclaiming. We have no research funding and do not want to create extra work for patients or staff that does not help them.
